title: Base expansions and recurring decimals
question: When does a fraction terminate or repeat in a chosen base?
summary: Long division is a finite remainder process. Termination is a denominator condition; a coprime denominator has a period measured by multiplicative order.
definition: Let \(B\ge2\) be an integer base and \(a/q\) a reduced rational number with \(q>0\). A terminating base-\(B\) expansion has only finitely many nonzero digits after the radix point.
For \(q\) coprime to \(B\), the multiplicative order \(\operatorname{ord}_q(B)\) is the least positive \(t\) with \(B^t\equiv1\pmod q\).
theorem: A reduced fraction \(a/q\), with \(q>0\), terminates in base \(B\ge2\) exactly when \(q\mid B^k\) for some \(k\ge0\). If \(q>1\) and \(\gcd(q,B)=1\), its long-division digits are purely periodic with least period \(\operatorname{ord}_q(B)\).
proof: A terminating expansion with at most \(k\) fractional digits equals an integer divided by \(B^k\). Since \(a/q\) is reduced, \(q\mid B^k\). Conversely, if \(B^k=qh\), then \(a/q=ah/B^k\), so a finite base-\(B\) expansion exists.

Long division updates a remainder by \(Br_j=q d_{j+1}+r_{j+1}\), with \(0\le r_{j+1}<q\). When \(q\) and \(B\) are coprime, a nonzero initial remainder never becomes zero, and \(r_j\equiv B^j a\pmod q\). Because \(a\) is coprime to \(q\), \(r_{j+t}=r_j\) exactly when \(B^t\equiv1\pmod q\). The deterministic digit update repeats at that point; no smaller period is possible because equal digit tails represent equal normalized remainders. \(\square\)

example.prompt: Compare the decimal behavior of \(1/8\) and \(1/7\).
steps: For \(1/7\), the successive nonzero remainders are \(1,3,2,6,4,5,1\).
Thus \(10^6\equiv1\pmod7\) with no earlier return to \(1\), and the decimal period is \(6\).
example.conclusion: The two denominators trigger different branches of the theorem.

practice.prompt: Classify the decimal expansion of \(1/12\): terminating, purely periodic, or eventually periodic? Explain the preperiod and period from exact remainders.
hints: The denominator contains factors shared with \(10\) and an odd factor coprime to \(10\).
Perform long division until a remainder repeats.
practice.answer: Long division gives \(1/12=0.08333\ldots\). The remainders after successive digits are \(10,4,4,\ldots\); after the two-digit preperiod \(08\), the digit \(3\) repeats with period \(1\). The coprime-order formula cannot be applied directly to \(q=12\).

caution: Remove denominator factors shared with the base before using an order formula. An eventually periodic expansion can have both a nonempty preperiod and a later cycle.
bridge: The remainder sequence is a finite state machine; the unit group controls the cycle when the denominator is coprime to the base.

title: Nonnegative linear equations and two coins
question: What is the largest amount two coprime coins cannot make?
summary: Integer solutions form a line; requiring nonnegative coefficients creates a final gap for coprime coin values.
definition: An amount \(N\ge0\) is representable by positive coin values \(a,b\) when \(N=ax+by\) for integers \(x,y\ge0\). The nonnegative restriction is stronger than integer solvability.
theorem: If integers \(a,b>1\) satisfy \(\gcd(a,b)=1\), the greatest nonrepresentable nonnegative integer is \(ab-a-b\). Every integer \(N>ab-a-b\) is representable.
proof: Suppose \(ab-a-b=ax+by\) for \(x,y\ge0\). Reducing modulo \(a\) gives \(b(y+1)\equiv0\pmod a\), so coprimality gives \(a\mid(y+1)\) and hence \(y\ge a-1\). Likewise \(x\ge b-1\). Then \(ax+by\ge a(b-1)+b(a-1)>ab-a-b\), a contradiction.

For \(N>ab-a-b\), choose the unique \(y\in\{0,\ldots,a-1\}\) with \(by\equiv N\pmod a\). Set \(x=(N-by)/a\), an integer. Since \(N\ge ab-a-b+1\) and \(by\le b(a-1)\), we have \(x>(-a)/a=-1\). Thus the integer \(x\ge0\), and \(y\ge0\), giving a representation. \(\square\)

example.prompt: Find the largest missing amount for coins \(4\) and \(7\).
steps: Modulo \(4\), any representation of \(17\) would require \(y\equiv3\pmod4\), giving \(7y\ge21>17\).
Every integer above \(17\) is representable: \(18=4+2\cdot7\), \(19=3\cdot4+7\), \(20=5\cdot4\), and \(21=3\cdot7\); then add \(4\) repeatedly.
example.conclusion: The obstruction and the coverage of all larger amounts are separate parts of the proof.

practice.prompt: Find the largest nonrepresentable amount for coins \(5\) and \(8\), and give representations of the next \(5\) amounts.
hints: One representation in each residue class modulo \(5\) suffices for all larger amounts.
practice.answer: The largest gap is \(5\cdot8-5-8=27\). The next amounts are \(28=4\cdot5+8\), \(29=5+3\cdot8\), \(30=6\cdot5\), \(31=3\cdot5+2\cdot8\), and \(32=4\cdot8\). Adding \(5\) gives every later amount.

caution: If \(\gcd(a,b)>1\), infinitely many positive targets outside that gcd's multiples are impossible, so no largest nonrepresentable target exists over all integers.
bridge: The residue choice in the proof is an exact finite certificate for nonnegative solvability, not merely a list of trial amounts.

title: Prime valuations of rational numbers
question: How many copies of one prime does a rational number carry?
summary: A prime valuation records exponents exactly, including negative exponents for rationals and an extended value for zero.
definition: For a prime \(p\) and nonzero integer \(n\), \(v_p(n)\) is the largest \(e\ge0\) for which \(p^e\mid n\). For nonzero rational \(a/b\), define \(v_p(a/b)=v_p(a)-v_p(b)\). Set \(v_p(0)=+\infty\), with the usual extended-order conventions.
The valuation measures divisibility by \(p\), not ordinary magnitude: a larger real number can have a smaller valuation.
theorem: For a prime \(p\), the rational valuation is independent of the chosen fraction representation. For nonzero rationals \(x,y\), \(v_p(xy)=v_p(x)+v_p(y)\). For rationals \(x,y\), \(v_p(x+y)\ge\min(v_p(x),v_p(y))\), with equality when the two valuations differ.
proof: If \(a/b=c/d\ne0\), then \(ad=bc\). Unique prime factorization of nonzero integers gives \(v_p(a)+v_p(d)=v_p(b)+v_p(c)\), hence \(v_p(a)-v_p(b)=v_p(c)-v_p(d)\). The same exponent addition proves the product rule.

For the sum, multiply \(x,y\) by a common denominator and factor out the smaller power of \(p\). If \(v_p(x)=r\le s=v_p(y)\), write \(x=p^r u\), \(y=p^r v\), where \(u,v\) are rationals with nonnegative valuations and \(v_p(u)=0\). Then \(x+y=p^r(u+v)\), and a common denominator prime to \(p\) shows \(v_p(u+v)\ge0\). If \(r<s\), then \(v_p(v)>0\), so reduction modulo \(p\) of the coprime-denominator numerators shows \(u+v\) is a unit and \(v_p(u+v)=0\). The cases with zero follow from \(+\infty\). \(\square\)

steps: Both \(9\) and \(18\) have valuation \(2\), but their sum is \(27\), with valuation \(3\).
example.conclusion: Equal input valuations may cancel and increase the valuation of a sum.

practice.prompt: Compute \(v_2(3/40)\) and \(v_2(3/40+1/8)\), and decide whether the unequal-valuation equality rule applies.
hints: Compare with \(v_2(1/8)=-3\) before claiming the unequal case.
practice.answer: Both summands have valuation \(-3\), so the unequal rule does not apply. Their sum is \(3/40+5/40=1/5\), with \(v_2(1/5)=0\). This is another strict increase.

caution: The equality case in the sum rule requires unequal valuations. Zero is assigned \(+\infty\), not a finite exponent, and fraction representation cannot change a valuation.
bridge: Valuation ledgers clarify lifting arguments and classify roots modulo prime powers by their divisibility depth.

title: Lifting exponents with exact hypotheses
question: When can a prime exponent be read from a difference of powers?
summary: The odd-prime lifting formula follows from a binomial valuation ledger; the prime two has a distinct even-exponent rule.
definition: For a prime \(p\), \(v_p(m)\) is the exponent of \(p\) in a nonzero integer \(m\). A lifting formula requires conditions on \(p,a,b,n\); it is not a universal identity for arbitrary power differences.
theorem: Let \(p\) be an odd prime, \(n\ge1\), and integers \(a,b\) satisfy \(p\mid(a-b)\) and \(p\nmid ab\). Then \(v_p(a^n-b^n)=v_p(a-b)+v_p(n)\), provided \(a^n\ne b^n\). If \(a,b\) are odd and \(n\) is even, then \(v_2(a^n-b^n)=v_2(a-b)+v_2(a+b)+v_2(n)-1\), provided the difference is nonzero.
proof: First let \(p\) be odd and set \(h=a-b\), \(r=v_p(h)\ge1\). In \(a^p-b^p=(b+h)^p-b^p\), the first term \(pb^{p-1}h\) has valuation \(r+1\), because \(p\nmid b\). Every middle term has valuation at least \(1+2r>r+1\), since \(p\mid\binom pj\) for \(1<j<p\). The final term \(h^p\) has valuation \(pr>r+1\). Hence \(v_p(a^p-b^p)=r+1\).

For an exponent \(m\) coprime to \(p\), factor \(a^m-b^m=(a-b)\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}a^{m-1-j}b^j\). Modulo \(p\), the sum is \(mb^{m-1}\ne0\), so its valuation is zero. Write \(n=p^s m\) with \(p\nmid m\). The coprime step keeps the valuation \(r\), and applying the prime-power step \(s\) times adds \(s=v_p(n)\).

For \(p=2\) and odd \(a,b\), write \(n=2^s m\) with \(s\ge1\) and \(m\) odd. The odd-exponent factorization shows \(v_2(a^m-b^m)=v_2(a-b)\) and \(v_2(a^m+b^m)=v_2(a+b)\). Squaring once gives the sum of these valuations. At every later squaring, both squared bases are \(1\pmod8\), so their sum is \(2\pmod8\) and contributes exactly one more factor of \(2\). There are \(s-1\) later squarings, yielding the stated formula. \(\square\)

example.prompt: Find \(v_3(7^9-1)\) and \(v_2(3^4-1)\) without expanding the large power.
steps: For the odd-prime case, \(3\mid(7-1)\), \(3\nmid7\), and \(v_3(7-1)=1\), so the valuation is \(1+v_3(9)=3\).
example.conclusion: The parity of the prime changes the exact formula.

practice.prompt: Show why the odd-prime formula cannot drop \(p\nmid ab\): compare its prediction for \(p=3,a=3,b=0,n=3\) with the actual valuation.
practice.answer: The actual value is \(v_3(27)=3\). The proposed right side is \(v_3(3)+v_3(3)=2\). The condition \(3\nmid ab\) fails because \(ab=0\), so the theorem does not apply.

caution: The case \(p=2\) needs its own formula, and \(a^n=b^n\) gives valuation \(+\infty\) rather than a finite equality. Always verify coprimality and parity hypotheses first.
bridge: The binomial ledger is a reusable proof pattern for lifting a congruence through prime powers.
